name: Flying Cards

lumenary.blurb: The picture dealt out as a grid of playing cards that hang in the air: each tilts and bobs on its own, throws a shadow on the table, and turns over to show its back when the cursor passes.

facts.era: Cards from the 9th century, card interfaces from the 2010s
facts.bestOn: Any picture; faces look best with few cards

why: Cut a picture into cards and it gains a third dimension for free. Each card can tilt, rise and turn over on its own, and because we know what a card is, a simple squeeze reads as a rotation and a shadow reads as height. The picture stays whole in the mind while it comes apart on the table.
how: Cut the picture into a grid of cards.
Deal them in a shuffled order from below the frame, each easing into place.
Tilt and lift every card with sine waves of its own speed and phase.
Draw a tilt as a squeeze by the cosine of the angle, and darken a card as it turns away.
Put a shadow under each card, further away and fainter the higher it floats.
Turn over the cards near the cursor to show their backs.
history: Playing cards are first recorded in China in the ninth century and reached Europe by the 1370s; the French suits of hearts, spades, diamonds and clubs date from about 1480. Patterned backs became usual in the nineteenth century so that marks and stains could not give a card away. On computers, the cascade of bouncing cards at the end of Solitaire in 1990 made card animation a small tradition of its own.
terms: Starting or ending a movement gradually instead of at a constant speed.
How far through its cycle a repeating motion is at a given moment.
Drawing a 3D object with no perspective, as if seen from very far away.
paragraphs: The picture is cut into a grid of cards, each showing its own part. On the deal, the cards are given a shuffled order and start one after another over a second and a half. Each flies from below the frame to its place along an ease-out cubic, turning as it goes. After that, nothing is simulated: every card’s pose is a formula of time with its own phase and speed, so the cards never fall into step.

A card is a flat rectangle turned about its vertical and horizontal axes and seen from straight ahead. Seen that way a rotation by an angle simply narrows the card by the cosine of the angle, so each card is drawn with two scale factors, and when the cosine about the vertical axis goes negative the back is drawn. The more a card is turned from the light the darker it gets. Its height above the table is another sine; the shadow is drawn further from the card and fainter as it rises. Near the cursor a flip value eases toward one and adds half a turn to the angle, then eases back more slowly.

equations.note: The deal: card i starts at time t_i and settles over three quarters of a second.
Width of a card as it turns about its vertical axis: T is the tilt slider, f the flip value (0 to 1).
The flip eases quickly over when the cursor is near and slowly back.

presets.text: Few large cards with a strong tilt feel like a magician’s spread.
Many small cards with no gap rebuild the picture as a mosaic.
A midnight table and a high float make the shadows the subject.
